paper_metadata.title: Evaluating Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Pricing Multi-Asset Basket Options

summary: This paper studies quantum amplitude estimation for pricing multi-asset basket options on real market data, using baskets of 3 to 9 assets and 1 to 8 uncertainty qubits per asset. Reported results show QAE can get close to Monte Carlo in some small cases, such as 3 assets at 8 qubits yielding 208.2440 versus Monte Carlo 208.25, but performance degrades or overshoots for larger baskets, and no practical quantum advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) workflow for pricing multi-asset basket options using real market data, evaluated by varying the number of uncertainty qubits for fixed basket sizes (3 to 9 assets) and comparing against classical Monte Carlo and Black-Scholes baselines.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for basket option pricing; includes state preparation, weighted adder, and LinearAmplitudeFunction payoff encoding

hyperparameters.uncertainty_qubits_per_asset: varied from 1 to 8 depending on basket size
hyperparameters.approximation_scaling_factor_c: reported as used in LinearAmplitudeFunction, value not specified
hyperparameters.strike_price_K: used in payoff mapping, values not fully enumerated

algorithm.parameter_initialization: State preparation from discretized lognormal distributions estimated from historical data; no trainable variational parameters

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each asset is discretized into 2^n grid points using n uncertainty qubits per asset; a weighted adder combines asset prices into a basket-price register; an objective qubit encodes the payoff via controlled rotations using a piecewise-linear approximation
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[max(0, A_d(T) - K)] where A_d(T)=sum_i w_i S_i(T) is the weighted basket price and K is the strike price
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: No explicit constraints beyond discretization and payoff thresholding; payoff condition encoded through LinearAmplitudeFunction and objective qubit

problem_instance.description: Pricing real-data multi-asset basket options with baskets of 3 to 9 equities; compare QAE-estimated final basket price / payoff against Monte Carlo and Black-Scholes
problem_instance.dataset_name: Yahoo Finance historical adjusted close prices

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Adjusted close prices; missing non-trading days excluded; log returns computed; mean and standard deviation estimated; parameters scaled to maturity T; small +5% shift to mean return; prices discretized into lognormal grids

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Retrieve daily adjusted close prices with yfinance; compute logarithmic returns; estimate mean return and volatility; scale by maturity T; add +5% mean shift; define price bounds as Si,0 exp(mu_i,T ± 3 sigma_i,T); discretize each asset into 2^n points; assume independent assets when forming joint distribution
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare QAE estimates to classical binned summation, Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 samples mentioned), and Black-Scholes; analyze impact of varying uncertainty qubits and varying asset count; report percentage deviation in Table I

hardware.framework: Qiskit (inferred from cited Qiskit Finance tutorial and Qiskit classes such as LogNormalDistribution, WeightedAdder, LinearAmplitudeFunction)

implementation_details.classical_solver: Monte Carlo simulation and Black-Scholes used as classical baselines; classical binned summation also used
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Historical market data loading, return estimation, scaling to maturity, discretization of lognormal distributions, basket construction
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Map estimated amplitude back to basket price / payoff; compute percentage deviation from classical final basket price

speedup_claims.conditions: in principle, for amplitude estimation sample complexity versus Monte Carlo
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the standard QAE advantage O(epsilon^-1) vs O(epsilon^-2), but the reported experiments focus on accuracy versus qubit count rather than runtime or oracle-query counts.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Quadratic improvement over Monte Carlo in principle: O(epsilon^-1) vs O(epsilon^-2) sample complexity for amplitude estimation
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Monte Carlo O(epsilon^-2) for target precision; basket pricing also grows rapidly with asset dimensionality

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; results are reported for 3- to 9-asset baskets with 1-8 uncertainty qubits per asset, but no runtime crossover analysis is given.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require substantially deeper circuits for state preparation, weighted addition, and amplitude estimation; the paper reports only theoretical O(epsilon^-1) vs O(epsilon^-2) scaling and no hardware execution data.
limiting_factors: No specific quantum hardware or noisy-device results
Circuit depth grows with uncertainty qubits and asset count
Classical Monte Carlo is used as the main benchmark and is competitive
Real-data loading and multi-asset state preparation are the main bottlenecks

notes: No specific QPU or simulator is named; hardware.type is left not_specified and framework is inferred from Qiskit Finance components mentioned in the methodology.
Exact total qubit count, circuit depth, gate counts, shots, and noise details are not explicitly reported in the provided text.
The paper reports varying uncertainty qubits per asset and basket sizes, but not a single fixed total qubit register size.

The paper reports that QAE can approach Monte Carlo for some settings, e.g. 3-asset basket at 8 qubits gives 208.2440 versus Monte Carlo 208.25, but larger baskets often overshoot or undershoot classical values.
No practical quantum advantage is demonstrated; the work is a benchmarking study with theoretical quadratic speedup claims.
